TITLE: Earnings call transcript: IQE posts strong H1 2024 growth, debt-free balance sheet

---
IQE said first-half revenue rose 43% year on year to GBP 64.6 million, helped by strong demand in wireless and photonics and by higher factory utilization, while the company also moved to a net cash position and eliminated bank debt. The shares were last up 0.63% at $47.75, compared with a previous close of $47.45, leaving the stock well above its 52-week low of $4.68 but below the $72.80 high.

Key Takeaways

Revenue climbed 43% to GBP 64.6 million in the first half of 2024.Wireless revenue rose 40% to GBP 26 million, while photonics revenue increased 45% to GBP 38.5 million.Adjusted EBITDA reached GBP 6 million as margins improved on better utilization and yields.IQE ended the period with GBP 41.6 million in cash and no bank debt.Management said long-term agreements are now central to the company’s commercial strategy.

Company Performance

IQE described the first half as a period of transformation following the close of its strategic review in April 2024. Chief Executive Jutta Bechwati said the company had shifted from a heavily leveraged business to one with a strong cash position and no bank debt.

Growth was broad-based. Wireless revenue increased 40% year on year, while photonics rose 45%. Management said the gains reflected stronger demand, better product mix and improved manufacturing performance across all sites.

The company also said it is seeing momentum in AI and data center-related applications, aerospace and defense, and wireless connectivity. Bechwati said IQE’s range of technologies gives it multiple routes into high-growth markets.

Financial Highlights

Revenue: GBP 64.6 million, up 43% year on year.Wireless revenue: GBP 26 million, up 40% year on year.Photonics revenue: GBP 38.5 million, up 45% year on year.Adjusted EBITDA: GBP 6 million.Adjusted operating cash flow: affected by a GBP 4 million working-capital outflow.Adjusted net cash position: GBP 30.2 million.Cash balance: GBP 41.6 million.Bank debt: zero.Margin trend: improved on better utilization, product mix and yield gains.

Earnings vs. Forecast

No EPS or revenue forecast was provided alongside the reported results, so a direct beat-or-miss comparison is not available. Even so, the operating picture was clearly stronger than a typical flat or low-growth period.

Revenue growth of 43% and the move to a debt-free balance sheet suggest a meaningful improvement in the business. The company also said the first half showed not only year-on-year growth but also half-on-half momentum, which points to continuing demand rather than a one-time lift.

Market Reaction

IQE shares were last quoted at $47.75, up 0.63% from the previous close of $47.45. That amounts to a gain of $0.30.

The move was modest, suggesting investors were positive on the results but not reacting with strong urgency. The stock remains far above its 52-week low, indicating a major recovery over the past year, though it still trades below the high end of the range. According to InvestingPro data, IQE has delivered a remarkable 849% return year-to-date and 452% over the past year, reflecting the dramatic turnaround in investor sentiment. This aligns with an InvestingPro Tip highlighting the stock’s high return over the last year. Investors seeking deeper insights can access 10+ additional ProTips, along with comprehensive financial metrics and Fair Value analysis on the platform.

No trading volume data were provided, so it is not possible to say whether the move came with unusual activity.

Outlook & Guidance

Management reiterated upgraded full-year guidance issued in July and said it remains confident in meeting that outlook. The company said the second half already reflects known supply risks, including substrate constraints and rare earth bottlenecks.

Looking further ahead, IQE said it expects at least 30% growth in 2026 and 2027, based on its current visibility and demand pipeline. The company also said it plans to update its strategy and reporting structure in 2027, with new long-term margin, revenue and growth targets.

IQE said it is converting existing tooling in the second half to increase Indium Phosphide capacity, but only where customer commitments support the investment. Management also said it is pursuing long-term agreements and, in some cases, customer prepayments to help fund expansion. The company’s 30% growth target for 2026-2027 appears achievable, with analysts forecasting 32% revenue growth in fiscal 2026, according to InvestingPro data. However, investors should note that InvestingPro’s Fair Value analysis suggests the stock may be overvalued at current levels—placing it among companies on the Most Overvalued list. The platform’s Financial Health Score rates IQE as "WEAK" at 1.75 out of 5, reflecting ongoing profitability challenges. For a complete analysis, IQE is one of 1,400+ US equities covered by InvestingPro’s comprehensive Pro Research Reports, which transform complex data into clear, actionable intelligence.

Executive Commentary

Bechwati said the company’s commercial model has changed sharply. “The major difference here is really that we’ve moved completely from a spot order approach to long-term agreements,” she said. “I think that really is so important because it gives us visibility on the utilization of our assets.”

She also pointed to the balance sheet turnaround. “We have gone from being a heavily leveraged business at the year-end to now being completely free of bank debt with a cash position of GBP 41.6 million,” she said.

On future demand, Bechwati said IQE is active in several fast-growing markets. “We are operating in the biggest and most important markets in the world, and they’re all growing rapidly,” she said, citing AI and data center supply chains in particular.

Risks and Challenges

Indium Phosphide substrate supply: Management said this is a key bottleneck for larger volume growth.Rare earth constraints: Supply issues could affect execution and capacity planning.6-inch substrate maturity: Yields remain less developed than on 3-inch and 4-inch substrates.Capacity expansion discipline: IQE says it will not add tooling without clear customer commitments.Guidance caution: The company said its outlook already reflects supply risks, which may limit upside in the near term.Margin pressure: Gross profit margins remain weak at just 1.39%, limiting profitability despite strong revenue growth.

Q&A

Analysts focused on long-term agreements, capacity expansion and supply constraints. Deutsche Bank’s Robert Sanders asked about the move from supplier-managed inventory to LTAs and whether customer prepayments could fund growth. Bechwati said prepayments are “definitely a mechanism” for funding expansion.

Sanders also asked about substrate technology, especially the difference between 4-inch and 6-inch Indium Phosphide. Bechwati said 4-inch remains the dominant market size, while 6-inch is growing but still maturing.

Other questions centered on pricing power, the Quintessence quantum dot laser deal, the company’s 2026 and 2027 outlook, and the status of a new CFO appointment. Bechwati said IQE is in a stronger position to seek better pricing, especially for bespoke products, but said long-term customer relationships matter more than short-term price increases.

The company also said it sees room for more market share gains, especially in AI-related applications, defense and satellite communications.

Full transcript - IQE PLC (IQE) H1 2026:Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Hello, everyone, and thank you for joining us for IQE’s interim results. I am proud to be able to present a really strong set of numbers, which exceeded our expectations and reflects the new transformed IQE. It’s been 133 days since we announced the conclusion of the strategic review and the investment from MACOM and other existing shareholders in April. I am very happy to say that it’s been an incredibly busy period since then, defined by some key commercial milestones and the signing of long-term agreements. It’s a fundamental change in how we operate as a business. I’ve always been clear that one of the things I wanted to achieve was greater visibility of orders and revenues, and that’s what these agreements are building towards.

As well as the multi-year agreements with MACOM, we’ve also signed a multi-year Indium Phosphide agreement with Tower Semiconductor, a $14 million production order with an AI and data center customer. Just last week, we announced a purchase agreement with Quintessence for Quantum Dot Laser epitaxy. These agreements reflect both the increasing demand in the market, especially from AI and data centers, but also how our strength and financial and operational position is enabling us to take advantage of those opportunities to expand our order book and to build visibility for the future. Let’s take a closer look at the progress IQE has made in first half. This slide gives you a clearer sense of how we play into our high growth end markets. I will not go through every point on this slide, but what I want you to take away from this is two key points.

First, we are operating in the biggest and most important markets in the world, and they’re all growing rapidly. This is visible to anyone who’s been looking at the global semiconductor ecosystem, in particular, the exponential growth of AI and data center related supply chains. Second, we have multiple routes into each of these segments. Our range of technologies mean that we can provide different solutions for these high growth sectors and access a broader pool of potential customers. Let me now touch on a few examples to bring this to life. Firstly, looking at IQE in the AI and data center market. As we’ve previously highlighted, we are seeing high demand for our Indium Phosphide and Gallium Arsenide optical interconnect technologies.

Layered on top of that are our gallium nitride on silicon MicroLED epitaxy for partners serving hyperscalers for high bandwidth, energy efficient data transfer in AI data centers, as well as gallium nitride on silicon power epitaxy, meeting the need for high efficiency power supply units within data center infrastructure. I would also like to bring your attention to Aerospace RF pipeline with new product qualifications and design wins across terrestrials, satellites, including low Earth orbit, and defense radar platforms. While at the same time, we’ve expanded our gallium antimonide infrared customer base into new geographies around the world. We take the same approach across all of our markets. Our critical position in these supply chains and our epitaxy expertise across a range of material systems is what makes IQE unique and the opportunities for us so compelling.

In order to capitalize on the strength of our technology and the market tailwinds, it is vital that our business is operating as effectively as possible, and this has always been a key priority for me. I am pleased to say that our focus on efficiency and operational excellence has already led to strong results with improvements in yields and production outputs across all of our sites. In order to build on the strong progress that we’ve made, Matt Geen has been appointed as our new Chief Operating Officer. Matt has been with our business for over 35 years and has significant experience in manufacturing and engineering leadership, and he will help us to strengthen operational oversight and drive continuous improvement.

A key element of how we’ve improved our model is related to the high volume of supply agreements that I spoke about earlier, as this has provided a strong future order visibility and allowed us to better optimize utilization of all of our assets. That is why I’m pleased to say that in the second half, we’ll be converting some of our existing tooling to increase capacity to meet the strong demand for Indium Phosphide. What you see here is a commercially driven model supported by our ability to scale to meet demand and an efficient approach to operations, all of which is flowing through to our bottom line. With that, I’d like to spend the next few slides walking through the financial performance of the half.

I’m really pleased to say that we’ve delivered first half revenue of GBP 64.6 million, which is an increase of 43% year-on-year. Wireless revenue was GBP 26 million, up 40% year-on-year, reflecting market share gains and increased sales of wireless mobile connectivity solutions across newly qualified customer platforms. On the right-hand side, you will see that Photonics revenue increased 45% year-on-year to GBP 38.5 million, driven by funding releases for certain U.S. military and defense programs, and continued growth in AI and data center-related markets. Overall, I’m happy to see continued growth, not just year-on-year, but half on half as well. Looking at our key financial highlights, you will see that our strong revenue growth and improved margins flow through to deliver GBP 6 million of adjusted EBITDA.

On margins, we saw good improvement driven by better utilization of our manufacturing capacity alongside a more favorable product mix, as Photonics made up a greater proportion of sales. Our adjusted operating cash flow was impacted by a working capital outflow of GBP 4 million, while our adjusted net cash position was GBP 30.2 million for the period following the conclusion of the group strategic review and receipt of fundraising proceeds. Turning to the net cash bridge. This chart highlights how significant the transformation for IQE has been. The conclusion of the strategic review has meant that we have gone from being a heavily leveraged business at the year-end to now being completely free of bank debt with a cash position of GBP 41.6 million. Overall, we have a fully funded balance sheet underpinned by a strong set of financials as we look ahead into the next phase of growth.

What you’ve seen is that first half was a really impressive performance for IQE. This was thanks to both the strong demand across all of our core segments and the improvements we’ve made to the business. Following our July trading update, where we’ve upgraded full-year guidance, we have seen the strong momentum continue into the second half of the year, which is expected to support growth throughout the remainder of 2026 and beyond. As a result, we are very confident of reaching our upgraded guidance. But in line with the way I’m running the business, this outlook reflects a prudent approach. While we are reiterating guidance today, we do also see potential for upside opportunities, thanks to the rising demand for optical communications for data center and AI infrastructure, which is underpinned by our recently signed supply agreements.

I would like to finish by talking about the future of the business, and I’m pleased that we’ve announced our intention to apply for IQE to list on the LSE main market. This is a momentous milestone for the business that has long been an ambition for us, and it’s a testament to the transformation of the business following the conclusion of the strategic review. This move would enable IQE to access a broader range of institutional capital, improve the liquidity of our shares, enhance our investor profile, and support our inclusion in the FTSE indices. We are targeting admission for first half 2027, but of course, we’ll update you on our progress in due course. To conclude, what does the strategy for the transformed IQE look like? There are three core elements I would like you to take away.

Firstly, we are a business that is supplying the highest growth market in the world with the broadest technology portfolio in the industry, which enables us to have multiple routes into each of these segments. Secondly, we have a new level of commercial focus and strategic customer alignment that is delivering long-term agreements and a growing order book, resulting in the strongest demand visibility that IQE has had in recent memory. And thirdly, I’ve embedded a relentless focus on operational excellence and continuous improvement, allowing our business to run as efficiently as possible for the benefit of our customers. Combined with our transformed financial position, this strategy is driving increasing revenues and margins, providing IQE with a clear path to sustainable growth. I am extremely excited about the future and the range of opportunities ahead. Thank you for your time, and I’d be happy to take any questions.

Conference Call Moderator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, if you would like to ask a question via the conference call, please press star one on your telephone keypad. We will pause for a brief moment. Thank you. We will take our first question from Robert Sanders of Deutsche Bank. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Yeah, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. Hi there, everyone. I have a quick question around the. If you could just contrast the approach that you’ve inherited on where you used to have supplier-managed inventory with large key accounts, which led to relatively low visibility to the long-term agreements that you’re now setting up. Is there any chance of receiving upfront prepayments to help to de-risk yourself?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Yes. Thank you, and thanks, Rob. The major difference here is really that we’ve moved completely from a spot order approach to long-term agreements. I think that really is so important because it gives us visibility on the utilization of our assets. It gives us visibility on how to better manage really any kind of supply into the sites and really enables us to plan for capacity expansion ahead of time. Absolutely, these kind of long-term agreements, if they do come with the need to increase our capacity, that would come with prepayments to really fund these expansions, and that is really important for us because we will also not expand capacity without a clear customer commitment and a clear visibility on what value is going to be driven with that expansion.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Is there a scenario where you could receive upfront prepayments, do you think, Jutta?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Absolutely. I think the prepayments, if you listen into some of our players in the same ecosystem, a lot of the capacity expansion right now is funded by customer prepayments, and we will utilize the same approach. Is it going to be true prepayments or different? There’s different methodologies as well, so it depends. Prepayments are definitely a mechanism for us to fund our growth.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Great. I have a follow-up question just around Quintessence. I am not that familiar with this area and how ready this company is to enter mass production. Obviously, you have received a volume order. At what stage of maturity is this company at or this technology at in terms of actually scaling up in big volumes? Thank you.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: I think that is a great question, actually, for Quintessence themselves, I would think. But we have been engaged with them for quite some time already, and I think they are ready for volume production. I think the main thing really is that this is going to be the next wave of innovation for data center applications and to increase efficiencies and really, again, a huge step up for data center technologies in general. But I do not have enough visibility or insight as to how ready they are truly for volume production.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Okay. Thank you very much. I will get back in the queue. Thanks.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Thank you.

Conference Call Moderator: Thank you. We will now take our next question from Harvey Robinson of Panmure Gordon. The line is open. Please go ahead.

Harvey Robinson, Analyst, Panmure Gordon: Thank you. I think probably following on from Robert’s question. Just on LTAs, what would good look like in terms of more agreements? Obviously, you have been pretty successful so far. Obviously, there is an expectation that you will continue to sign LTAs. Related to that, obviously, CapEx is pretty light in the first half. Obviously, given where the business is, we all are aware of unutilized space within Newport. What would the conditions be in terms of customer agreements, customer visibility for you to start building out that capacity?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Thanks, Harvey. First, on the LTAs. I think, as I have mentioned, the LTAs are extremely important and a cornerstone of our new strategy for the company to really get visibility and to really get clear insights of capacity requirements and capacity needs. We are working closely with a lot of customers on additional agreements. Some of these agreements will come with announcements, others will not. We will try to add as much transparency on LTAs as we can. I think that that is really important for us to note is that there is quite a bit in the pipeline right now that we are working on and we are quite excited about. That secondly then goes to your next question on CapEx and that expansion. As I have mentioned, any kind of capacity expansion will have to come with customer commitments and agreements.

The LTAs are the foundation for the capacity expansion, and only with that clarity and with that certainty of that demand will we add more tooling into, for example, the site in Newport. Yes, we do still have ample clean room space to add capacity. This is a huge advantage for us because we can scale up rather quickly compared to others because we already have the infrastructure to house these reactors.

Harvey Robinson, Analyst, Panmure Gordon: Thank you. That is perfect. Thank you.

Conference Call Moderator: Thank you. We have no further questions from the line. I will now hand over to Chloe for webcast questions.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Thank you. I will now run through the questions submitted through the webcast. Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Okay, how much time do I have? I think it is extremely important to really point out IQE’s diversified portfolio. I think our current structure of reporting doesn’t really do it justice if you just look at wireless and photonics. This is really why we have added the additional dimensions in the presentation to highlight really our diverse footprint, not just on a geopolitical point of view, but also really on a portfolio manner. In just AI data center, I just want to point out again, data centers is one component of AI, but we are really playing into all spaces of AI from really the rack to the edge. Data centers is just one component of where we are supporting AI.

Onto aerospace and defense, I think it is extremely important to highlight that we have been a very substantial part of the overall military and defense ecosystem in the U.S. already, especially with our infrared sensing technology based on our gallium antimonide technologies. We have been a very important partner of the prime companies that are playing in that space. For the communication infrastructure on, for example, our RF technology, where we have radio frequency and power networks, we are playing into the radar space there and satellite, as well as the overall infrastructure for the networks there. I think it is really important to highlight our diverse footprint and diverse portfolio offerings.

We do want to give you more of that insight, really, again, with the presentation that we have had, but also in next year, where we want to give you more of an opportunity to highlight some of the growth opportunities in these different sectors and also change really the way that we are reporting our results to showcase more of that diverse footprint.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Thank you. The second question is, please could you remind us how comfortable you feel about the 2026 outlook, given the noise around supply shortage?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: The supply shortage is an extremely important point for us, where we have to keep an eye on that. Everybody is quite aware of the fact that there is substrate supply concerns, as well as rare earth bottlenecks that are highlighted in each of the calls that you are seeing in the industry. What we are doing here is really ensuring that we are working with the suppliers in each of these segments to mitigate some of the risk and the exposures that we have. But also, really the second half outlook already reflects these risks that we are seeing to ensure that we are monitoring that very closely and not over-committing to a number that we will not be able to hit.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: How much CapEx will be needed to convert your machines to meet Indium Phosphide demand?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: That’s a really good question. It really depends on the reactor itself, so it’s hard to pinpoint the exact amount there. It’s definitely insignificant compared to the cost of a new reactor. The main investment really is mainly the downtime of the tool, because you actually take it off of production for a time, and that obviously is opportunity costs that are lost. I think it’s still a worthwhile investment. Even with that minimal investment, we are still not converting tools without customer commitments and secured demand on these tools.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Where are you with the appointment of a new CFO?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Very good question. It’s an ongoing process. We are really making good progress on that, and we will update you in due course.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Can you enlighten us on the margin improvements made in H1, and do you have any targets going forward?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: The main improvements that we’ve seen in H1 were really driven by our operational efficiencies and with the utilization of the existing assets. I think that is a key thing that we are able to achieve the revenue expansion, really, with the existing assets. Also, additional efforts were driven by yield improvements and activities around really truly reestablishing operational excellence in all of our areas. We are seeing the results of these efforts that have been put into place over the last 18 months.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Are there any hopes that IQE can still attract CHIPS funding in the U.S.?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: That’s a really good question. The activities with governments have not just been limited to the U.S. We are working actively across all regions to ensure that we are taking advantage of programs that have been offered and also potentially looking into funding opportunities for very discrete projects. There also, we will keep you posted, but I think it’s an ongoing activity that we are constantly in touch with the various organizations with.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Is there room for IQE to benefit from divestments, i.e., the sale of the factory in Taiwan? Is the sale of part of the business still in scope?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: To take a step back. When we introduced the thought of selling Taiwan, that was driven of the necessity, looking at our balance sheet, and really the need to fund the existing debt structure. Luckily, we are now in a very transformed situation. There is no need to sell anything right now to strengthen our balance sheet. We have an extremely healthy balance sheet right now, and actually the diverse footprint, as such, the inclusion of Taiwan enables us really to play into geopolitical situations that we can deliver into all existing markets and really offset some of the constraints that others would be seeing without such a diverse geopolitical footprint. So no, we are not looking into selling anything at the moment, and not in the foreseeable future either.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: What progress, if any, can you report on the ULTRARAM project last reported in the 16th of June 2025 RNS announcement?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: The ULTRARAM program is something that showcases our rich R&D pipeline. We are still progressing with that, and we will keep you on any kind of volume production in due course. But I think the main thing really is that we keep investing into R&D opportunities so that we can really take advantage of the next wave of innovation coming our way.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: I noticed at the back end of your release today, as part of the going concern statement, you talk about at least 30% growth in both 2026 and 2027. You are not guiding to 2027 today, and the analysts have extrapolated H2 expectations growth into 2027. We understand the prudence. What is the thinking around timing of revising the outlook? Is it more LTAs or is it when you have to?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: It is a combination of things. I think really the visibility for us with LTAs are really important to have that in place and more of the really demand security. We also need to work through some of the bottlenecks that I have just described with the Indium Phosphide, especially Indium Phosphide substrate constraints that we have. So a combination of these factors will lead us then to update the market when we can.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Could you comment on the competitive environment? Is there any change there? It feels like in some areas you are gaining market share.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: That is certainly the goal, gaining market share. The mobility right now that we are seeing in the AI space, in the ecosystem, it is something that we are working very closely with all different partners on. That certainly could result in additional market share, and we will update the market as soon as we can give you more insights on that.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Can you please shed some light on possible revenues and progress related to GaN power and MicroLED?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: GaN power, I think we’ve highlighted that a few years back as the major opportunity within the GaN program itself. I think from a technology perspective, GaN power has shifted to the right, but we are now seeing really significant pickup on that opportunity. MicroLED as part of also the overall GaN technology application footprint is really gaining more and more momentum on that and really is almost surpassing the GaN power application, with various solutions really that we are supporting in the MicroLED space. I think there is various applications that we are supporting. It’s great to see that pick up and we’ve got momentum in that space.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Are you seeing an ability to increase pricing power?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: As you can imagine, our balance sheet in the past has not been truly the best starting point for any negotiations when it comes to customer engagements. However, with our new strategy around LTAs customer engagement, really the main thing is that we have a strategic partnership with the customers. A price increase with that is one of the levers that we are pulling, but really the strategic importance of a long-term relationship overtakes more of the short-term pricing increases. However, I do believe that we are in a much better position really to demand higher pricing, especially for our bespoke solutions. We will definitely take advantage of that going forward.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: What is the company’s strategy in respect to Indium Phosphide substrates?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Indium Phosphide substrates, as I have mentioned, and also as you can see from other publications when you look at the results from various players in the industry, Indium Phosphide substrates are becoming some of the bottlenecks around significant volume increases. Therefore, we are working closely with everybody in the industry and with all partners to ensure that we are locking in volume allocations to secure our demand that we are currently seeing with our customers. However, this is an ongoing activity that we are monitoring very closely because this is something that we are seeing as a bottleneck and also as a risk. This is a high item on our list of reviewing that.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Do you have a view about what margins should be for IQE in the long term?

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: That is a really good question, and we will update our outlook and our targets in any strategy reset that we will provide in 2027. I think it is really important to have the dust settle a bit on our new transformed company. As such, we are reviewing our strategy right now, putting together a five-year plan, and we will then update the market with our newly formed segment reporting as well as then also setting more long-term targets on margins, revenue, and growth.

Chloe, Webcast Question Moderator: Thank you very much, Jutta. I think we’re going to close the questions there.

Conference Call Moderator: Thank you. We’ll take our next follow-up question from Robert Sanders of Deutsche Bank. Your line is open. Please go ahead.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Yeah. Thanks. Just one quick follow-up question on 6-inch versus 4-inch. It sounds like you have quite a strong capability to convert Aixtron G4 tools to 6-inch for Indium Phosphide. However, it sounds like the industry is struggling with 6-inch line yields as opposed to epi yields. If that situation drags on, would you be more happy because 4-inch substrates are more available? Or would you be kind of unhappy because 6-inch is where you have more of a kind of competitive edge? Thanks.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Thanks, Rob. First of all, just to clarify, we are converting technology. We are converting tools from Gallium Arsenide, for example, to Indium Phosphide. That doesn’t necessarily come with a dimension conversion. That can still be within 4-inch, especially since 4-inch is still the very dominant substrate in the market. Right now, if I look at the overall 4-inch, the distribution of the Indium Phosphide substrates right now, 3-inch is still very dominant. Then it’s 4-inch with almost half of the volume driven by 4-inch, and only then comes 6-inch as the fastest-growing sort of diameter, and it’s scaling right now. I think the 6-inch still is something that obviously we can support, but it’s still something that the maturity needs to be, and also the yield with that obviously needs to improve, as you’ve pointed out.

Overall, we are able to support 3, 4-inch, and then going into 6-inch as well. But I think really from a market pool right now, we are not seeing truly the really demand on 6-inch yet.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Got it. Can you just contrast the tightness of substrates across those three diameters? That would be great, and then I will leave you alone. Thanks a lot.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: I think that is very difficult for us to assess right now. I think mainly when we look at maturity, which is usually where the volume plays, 3-inch definitely would be there. But I think 4-inch is where the market is going to, but it is difficult to say, okay, where exactly the pinch points are. It also depends really on the actual substrate itself because there is different types of substrates too. So it is multiple dimensions that come into play when you look at the constraints, market constraints of substrates.

Robert Sanders, Analyst, Deutsche Bank: Perfect. Thanks a lot, Jutta.

Jutta Bechwati, CEO, IQE: Thank you.
